system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma, ulcerative colitis, asthma, and a history of DVT/PE was admitted for her 12th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She tolerated the treatment well, with expected mild transaminitis and manageable nausea. An MRI showed stable remission of her lymphoma. She disclosed a recent suicide attempt by oxycodone overdose, prompting a psychiatry consultation. Due to ongoing depressive symptoms and inadequate outpatient mental health resources, she was deemed unsafe for discharge home and arranged for transfer to an inpatient psychiatric facility. Her anticoagulation was changed from enoxaparin to aspirin per neuro-oncology recommendation. Gabapentin was increased for chronic right foot pain, and citalopram was uptitrated to 40mg daily. She cleared methotrexate adequately and was transferred to extended psychiatric care in stable condition.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Poisoning by other opiates and related narcotics
Suicide and self-inflicted poisoning by analgesics, antipyretics, and antirheumatics
Antineoplastic and immunosuppressive drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Other nonspecific abnormal serum enzyme levels

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ woman, with CNS lymphoma.  Now with new frontal
headache.

COMPARISON:  Multiple prior studies with the latest MR head on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Multiplanar, multisequence T1- and T2-weighted MR images were
acquired through the head before and after administration of IV gadolinium
contrast.  Diffusion-weighted images and ADC maps were also obtained.

FINDINGS:  Compared to the most recent study on ___, there are
no significant post-treatment changes centered in the right frontal lobe. 
Again noted is right frontal and insular encephalomalacia with old blood
products.  A tiny DWI bright focus in the right frontal region (image 502:22),
unchanged and representing artifacts from the old hemorrhage.  There is
unchanged right frontovertex craniotomy defect.

Ex vacuo dilatation of the right frontal horn is again noted.  There is no
shift of normally midline structures.  There is no evidence of new hemorrhage
or acute infarction.  Major vascular flow voids are preserved.

In the paranasal sinuses, there is interval increase of aerosolized fluid in
the right frontal sinus with superimposed mucosal thickening.  There is
interval resolution of left frontal mucosal thickening.

A moderate-sized mucus retention cyst is again noted in the anterolateral wall
of the right maxillary sinus.  There is interval increased of right maxillary
sinus fluid.

Moderate ethmoidal opacification is unchanged.  The sphenoid sinuses are
clear.  A small amount of retention fluid is noted in the right mastoid air
cells.  

The globes are grossly unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Similar post-treatment changes in the right insular and frontal lobe,
without new abnormal enhancement or new masses.  No acute infarct or new
intracranial hemorrhage.

2.  Interval worsening of the right frontal and maxillary sinus disease. 
Interval clearing of the left frontal sinus mucosal thickening.  Persistent
moderate ethmoidal opacification.  The new frontal headache could be secondary
to the interval worsening of the right-sided paranasal sinus disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here today for your 13th cycle of high-dose methotrexate for your CNS lymphoma, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been doing this every month now. I hope this one goes as smoothly as the last few.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do our best. I see from your record that last time, you were struggling with depression and had a difficult episode. How have you been feeling emotionally since then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, actually. I went to a short rehab program and have been seeing my psychiatrist regularly. I’m still on citalopram, 40 mg daily, and it’s helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Mental health is just as important as physical health, especially with everything you’re managing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m trying to stay on top of it. But I have been getting these headaches lately—frontal, on both sides. They started about two weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see that in your chart. They’re not constant, and Tylenol helps a little?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They don’t wake me up at night, and I don’t have any vision changes or nausea with them. Just annoying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get an MRI today to check your brain and make sure there’s no change in your lymphoma. Headaches can sometimes be a sign, but they can also be from other things like sinus issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve also been having that same burning pain in my right foot. It’s been going up my leg too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s been chronic for a while. We’ve done MRIs, ultrasounds, even a spinal tap—all normal. We’ll keep you on gabapentin, and we can adjust the dose if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on 800 mg three times a day now. Is that the max?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can go higher, but we’ll see how you do. We also need to be careful with pain meds because of your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. My husband is helping me with any oxycodone I take, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good plan. We’ll continue that support. Now, your chemotherapy will start soon. We’ll give you IV fluids to protect your kidneys and help flush the methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the leucovorin the next day, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. 24 hours after the chemo, we’ll start leucovorin to rescue your healthy cells. We’ll also give you anti-nausea meds—prochlorperazine—as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually get a little nauseous, so I’ll take that if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. Also, your asthma is stable? Still using your inhalers?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, fluticasone-salmeterol twice a day and montelukast at night. I’ve used albuterol once this week, but not much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep those going. One more thing—we’re holding your mesalamine for ulcerative colitis during this admission because it can interact with methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Should I stop it at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just during the chemo days. You can restart it after you’re done clearing the methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood work looks okay for the chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your labs this morning were good. Kidney function is normal, and your liver enzymes are baseline. Creatinine clearance is over 130, so we’re safe to proceed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I always worry about the liver part.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect mild transaminitis—it’s common with this treatment—but we monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chemotherapy is starting now. The nurse will be in shortly to begin the infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your MRI results are back. I have good news—no signs of lymphoma progression. The changes in your brain are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, thank goodness. So what’s causing the headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI shows increased mucosal thickening in your right frontal and maxillary sinuses. That’s likely what’s causing the headaches—mild sinusitis, not infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. It’s not bacterial. We’ll treat it with rest, fluids, and pain relief. We can give you a small prescription of oxycodone for breakthrough pain, but only as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll be careful with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today? Any nausea or headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nauseous this morning. I took the prochlorperazine. Headache is mild.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. We’ll keep the anti-nausea meds available. Your urine output is good, and pH is alkaline—perfect for clearing the methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When do I get the leucovorin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later this morning, about 24 hours after the chemo started. We’ll give it orally every six hours for several doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—your latest labs are stable. No kidney issues, and liver enzymes are only slightly elevated, which we expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m feeling a bit more energy today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Will I be able to manage the pain at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with your regular gabapentin—800 mg three times a day—and a small supply of oxycodone, 10 mg every four hours as needed for severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only 20 pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just for breakthrough pain. We want to minimize risk, especially given your history. Your husband will help monitor it, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he will. That’s fine. And my aspirin? I was on enoxaparin before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. Your neuro-oncologist recommended switching from enoxaparin to aspirin for your history of DVT and PE. It’s safer with your condition. We’ll restart your 325 mg daily at discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. Your labs are stable, you’ve tolerated the chemo, and your mental status is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When do I come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In one month for your next cycle. In the meantime, keep using your asthma meds, take the aspirin daily, and continue gabapentin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if the headaches come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use Tylenol first. If it’s severe, you can take one oxycodone, but don’t exceed the dose. And call your neuro-oncologist if they worsen or don’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Keep up with your psychiatric follow-up too. We’re all here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel more stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you next month.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old woman with primary central nervous system lymphoma, ulcerative colitis, asthma, and a history of DVT/PE was admitted for her 13th cycle of high-dose methotrexate chemotherapy. She tolerated the treatment well with only mild nausea, managed with anti-emetics. She reported a two-week history of frontal headaches, and an MRI showed no progression of her lymphoma but revealed worsening mucosal thickening in the right frontal and maxillary sinuses, likely contributing to her headaches. No antibiotics were needed. She remained emotionally stable on citalopram, with no signs of active depression. Her chronic right foot pain persisted, and she was discharged with continued gabapentin and a limited supply of oxycodone for breakthrough pain. Anticoagulation was transitioned from enoxaparin to aspirin per neuro-oncology guidance. She cleared methotrexate without renal or hepatic complications and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up scheduled in one month.
problems: Primary central nervous system lymphoma, unspecified site, extranodal and solid organ sites
